name: Leather work and welding gloves
summary: Gloves of cowhide, goatskin, pigskin or similar leather for rough handling, sparks and moderate heat, including long welding gauntlets.
uses: Rough objects, chips, blows, sparks and moderate heat (OSHA 3151)
Sharp edges: leather alone is not cut-resistant and gives real cut protection only with a cut-resistant liner; use cut gloves for sheet metal and glass (SUPERIOR CUT)
Welding: EN 12477 Type A for general welding and cutting, Type B where more dexterity is needed, as for TIG (SATRA EN 12477); thick leather for stick and MIG (AWS PPE)
No chemical protection: leather and fabric gloves absorb chemicals and are not chemical-resistant (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES)
No electrical protection: OSHA lists insulating rubber gloves as their own type, and ASTM F696 leather covers over them give mechanical protection only (OSHA 3151, ASTM F696)

No gloves at drill presses, lathes, mills, band saws or bench grinders, or near any shaft, roller or belt that could pull one in (OSHA 3170, CCOHS DRILL PRESS, CCOHS LATHES, CCOHS MILLING, CCOHS BENCH GRINDERS, CCOHS METALWORKING, OSHA BAND SAW)

Hand-held grinders and winch rope are the exceptions: CCOHS names tight-fitting gloves for grinder attachments, Makita lists gloves for its angle grinder, and Warn calls for heavy leather gloves on winch rope (CCOHS GRINDER ATTACHMENTS, MAKITA GA4032, WARN RIGGING)
identify: Grain leather is the smooth outer side of the hide; split is the rough, suede-like layer. Welding gloves often have split leather on the back and cuff to block sparks and grain on the palm; grain sheds molten metal better (AWS PPE). Thin goat, deer or sheep skin gives the tight fit TIG welders need (AWS PPE). For heat, CCOHS puts chrome-tanned leather at up to about 100 °C, heat-resistant or lined leather higher, and aluminised gloves above 350 °C (CCOHS GLOVES). European marks: EN 12477 welding gloves are Type A (more protection, less dexterity) or Type B (more dexterity, as for TIG) (SATRA EN 12477). The EN 407 flame symbol has six digits: limited flame spread, contact heat (levels 1 to 4 for 100, 250, 350, 500 °C for at least 15 seconds), convective heat, radiant heat, small splashes and large molten metal; X means not tested. A plain heat symbol instead of the flame means the maker makes no flame claim, as with oven gloves (EJENDALS EN 407). EN 388 and ANSI/ISEA 105 marks give cut levels (SUPERIOR CUT). Linemen's leather protectors made to ASTM F696 go over rubber insulating gloves and give mechanical protection only (ASTM F696). A glove with no marks has no stated rating.
test: Look for holes, burned-through spots, split seams, and palms or fingertips worn thin; a welding glove with a hole lets in spatter. Reject leather that is cracked, stiff and brittle, or soaked with oil, fuel or chemicals; leather and fabric gloves absorb chemicals (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES). Shake them out before putting them on. Fit: welding gloves should cover the hand, wrist and lower forearm and work with your sleeve, over or under it (AWS PPE). For welding, keep them dry: don't change an electrode with a wet glove, and wear rubber gloves under the leather in wet or humid conditions (CCOHS WELDING). Dry hands and dry gloves matter because a damp body has less resistance to shock (CCOHS WELDING). For hot parts, check the rating first: plain chrome-tanned leather is listed only up to about 100 °C (CCOHS GLOVES). Take them off at a drill press, lathe, mill, band saw or bench grinder, and near any shaft, roller or belt that can catch a glove (OSHA 3170, CCOHS DRILL PRESS, CCOHS METALWORKING); hand-held grinders and winch rope are the exceptions.

decay.note: Estimate. Leather keeps for years if stored dry; damp storage brings mould and rot, and stitching and linings usually give out before the hide.

improvise: Better than nothing for rough handling: sturdy canvas gloves are in the same OSHA 3151 group as leather, for rough handling and sustained heat (OSHA 3151). Plain fabric gloves are not enough for rough, sharp or heavy material (OSHA 3151). For hot work, aramid or terry cloth gloves handle up to about 100 to 200 °C (CCOHS GLOVES). Oven gloves are for contact heat only, not flame or molten metal (EJENDALS EN 407). A glove without the EN 407 flame mark makes no claim for flame or molten metal (EJENDALS EN 407). Don't weld in plain work gloves: welding gloves are made to block sparks and molten metal (AWS PPE). Useless: leather of any kind against chemicals, which it soaks up (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES), and against live wiring, where OSHA wants the power off first and only qualified people on live parts (OSHA 1910.333).
